targets.approach: From the Lower Goodell Creek trailhead, day one covers more than six miles and 6,000 feet of elevation gain to a col near the Chopping Block. Day two crosses snow, slabs, and talus through Crescent Creek Basin, then crampons up to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, followed by one rappel down onto the Mustard Glacier to reach the base of the North Buttress.
targets.name: North Buttress (Thread of Gneiss)

targets.approach: From a camp on the Chopping Block ridge, traverse Crescent Creek Basin and climb to the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col, then descend its north side onto the Mustard Glacier; the couloir starts roughly 1,000 ft below the col and tops out at the Eye Col between the two Needles. The usual way down is by the gullies on the south side of the Eye Col back into Crescent Creek Basin.
targets.name: Thread of Ice

targets.approach: North-northeast via glacier traversals. From Boston Basin parking, hike to Boston Basin high camp (~6400 ft). Traverse moraine and west edge of Quien Sabe Glacier to 7,500 ft. Climb to Sharkfin Col (7,720 ft).
targets.descent: Reverse toward the West Ridge notch and descend the standard West Ridge couloir, or rappel the climbed line as appropriate.
targets.descent_text: Descend via the West Ridge couloir (the standard Forbidden descent) back into Boston Basin.
targets.name: North Ridge

targets.approach: From the South Tieton Creek/Conrad Meadows Trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the east side of Conrad Glacier to a saddle around 7,200 ft.
targets.descent: Descend the ascent route back over the saddle and down Conrad Glacier.
targets.descent_text: Reverse the traverse from Meade Glacier back over the ~7,200 ft saddle and down Conrad Glacier to Conrad Meadows.
targets.name: Conrad Glacier

wa_der_dihedral.approach: Approach as for Backbone Ridge and Serpentine Arete: from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3-4.4 miles, ~2,200 ft gain, 2-2.5 hours). From the lake, follow the lateral moraine/talus below Dragontail's north face as for Backbone Ridge, but Der Dihedral's start is lower on the face and a couple of ridgelines short of (east/left of, and below) Backbone Ridge proper - it is not as well-cairned or as heavily travelled as the Backbone/Serpentine approach. Look for a clean left-facing dihedral a pitch or two up the initial ridge; because the route sees little traffic, budget extra time for route-finding to the exact start from the moraine (scanning from lake level with binoculars helps). Total approach roughly 3-3.5 hours from the trailhead.
wa_der_dihedral.descent_text: There is almost no descent-specific beta for Der Dihedral beyond the fact that it joins the 1972 NE Arete to finish. Since the route tops out on the same upper mountain terrain as Backbone Ridge, the standard descent is the same walk-off used for that route and for the summit generally: scramble/snow traverse southeast to a saddle, then east across the long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, and down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer. A rappel alternative exists on Backbone Ridge's finish for icy conditions (ledges below the summit to a rap station, two rappels to a ledge system, then a scramble north to Aasgard Pass) - if Der Dihedral's top-out lands near that same station it may be usable, but this has not been confirmed for this route, so plan on the standard walk-off by default.
wa_der_dihedral.name: Der Dihedral

wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Colchuck Lake Trail (~4 mi, 2,280 ft gain) → around the lake and up the moraine to the route base (roughly 200 ft left of Serpentine Arête); initial bushwhacking on brushy ledges until the party cliffs out and traverses up/right toward the ridge crest.
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.descent_text: Most parties descend the east ledges and sandy summit gully toward Aasgard Pass and down to Colchuck Lake. When the upper descent gully is icy (common late season), rappel instead — two rappels on a 70m rope (60m works) using rock anchors to avoid the ice slope, with a documented rappel station near 47.479°N, 120.832°W. Watch for loose rock and verify anchor integrity on any rappel here — parties have found the anchors below the first station poor enough to turn round and downclimb instead, and the second rappel runs directly over a loose flake big enough to kill, with the standard walking descent passing below it.
wa_dragontail_peak_backbone_ridge.name: Backbone Ridge

wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.approach: From Colchuck Lake's west side trail, follow cairns up the climbers' trail into Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in 0.75 mile. At the pass, head right/south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin (typically snow-covered through late July, a mellow, low-crevasse slope) to the saddle on the east ridge, then a class-3 scramble/ridge walk to the summit.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.descent_text: It is a common and dangerous mistake for fatigued parties to veer too far climber's-right on the Aasgard Pass descent into steep, cliffed-out terrain — stay on the cairned line trending climber's-left. A slide on the steep upper pass could carry a climber into boulders below; icy conditions here have contributed to serious falls and fatalities.
wa_dragontail_peak_east_ridge_aasgard_pa.name: East Ridge via Aasgard Pass Route

wa_dragontail_peak_r2.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.3-4.4 miles, ~2,200 ft gain). This route is typically climbed in winter/spring ice conditions, so expect a longer, harder approach with real avalanche exposure - many parties snowshoe or ski/skin in and camp near the lake rather than climbing car-to-car. From the lake, ascend talus/snow along the moraine below the north face toward the gap between the Triple Couloirs start (further left/west) and Backbone Ridge/the Fin (further right/east) - Gerber-Sink takes the lowest point on Dragontail's north face ('nordwand'), following runnels connecting snow bands right of center for 1,000+ ft of ice/neve, finishing in the third of the Triple Couloirs. Approach time in winter conditions is 3-5 hours from the lake depending on snowpack; moving as a rope team across the apron below the face is prudent given overhead rock/icefall hazard.
wa_dragontail_peak_r2.descent_text: Parties who top out into the upper Triple Couloirs exit typically continue, unroped, down the standard boot-packed couloir/gully system used to descend Triple Couloirs, then continue to Aasgard Pass and descend its snow slope (glissading is common) back to Colchuck Lake - one documented winter ascent finished exactly this way, unroped after the couloir and glissading most of Aasgard Pass. This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent, on every ascent on record. Crampons and an axe are standard for the whole descent; both the couloir exit and Aasgard Pass carry avalanche, rockfall, and icefall hazard, so timing (early starts, stable snowpack) matters more than technical descent gear. No rappels are recorded for a completed ascent, though a party that gets high on the face but cannot continue over the top could face a difficult retreat down steep ice/mixed terrain that might require an improvised v-thread or gear rappel - this is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for on a Grade IV ice/mixed route.
wa_dragontail_peak_r2.name: Gerber-Sink

wa_dragontail_peak_r3.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3-4.4 miles and about 2,200 ft of gain (2-2.5 hours). Unlike the Aasgard Pass routes, continue around the lake's west/south side toward the Colchuck Glacier below the Colchuck-Dragontail col. Ascend talus and then the glacier itself - early season mostly snow, becoming firmer neve/ice with exposed talus by mid-to-late season; the glacier's east lobe is generally reported free of significant crevasses but can be hard enough to want crampons and an axe. Climb the glacier to Colchuck Col; the couloir entrance for Pandora's Box (the W Couloir) is a couple hundred feet left (east) of the col itself and climbs to a notch in the ridge. Total approach 3-4 hours. Hazards: firm morning snow/ice on the glacier approach, and the couloir is a fall-line funnel for rockfall/icefall from the terrain above, so an early start to beat sun-loosened debris and softening snow matters.
wa_dragontail_peak_r3.descent_text: From the top of the couloir/Pandora's Box, descend left and traverse northeast to the true summit (some parties rope up for this exposed traverse), or alternatively exit about 30 ft below the notch, scramble Class 4 rock roughly 20 ft, and follow the ridge left to the top. From the summit, the standard descent is southeast to a saddle, then east across a long snow slope to Aasgard Pass, then down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) to Colchuck Lake - stay climbers' left near the granite walls and beware drifting climbers' right into cliffs. Crampons/axe are recommended into mid-summer; early season the descent can largely be glissaded. No rappels are needed on this standard summit-and-Aasgard-Pass finish. If a party instead retreats directly back down the couloir rather than topping out, downclimbing steep snow/ice or building an improvised rappel off natural gear (slung chockstones or horns) in the couloir could become necessary - this specific scenario is not recorded anywhere but is a reasonable contingency to plan for in a steep snow couloir.
wa_dragontail_peak_r3.name: Pandora's Box (W Couloir)

wa_dragontail_peak_r4.approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead to Colchuck Lake (4.5 mi, ~2,000 ft gain), then approach the base of the north face aiming for the lowest rock protrusion near the middle of the wall to find the Hidden Couloir entrance around 6,400 ft.
wa_dragontail_peak_r4.descent_text: From the top of the third couloir, a short snow scramble reaches the summit. Traverse to the true summit, then make a long descending traverse across the upper snowfields toward Asgard Pass, and descend the pass's gully back to the frozen/open lake and the approach trail.
wa_dragontail_peak_r4.name: Triple Couloirs

wa_dragontail_peak_serpentine_arete.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail ~4 mi / 2,280 ft gain to Colchuck Lake (5,574 ft). Round the lake's west shore to its south end, boulder-hop onto the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine, and traverse it toward the orange-colored rock marking the route start; 4th-class ledges lead up to a snow finger and the base of the technical climbing. Roughly 3 hours car-to-base at a brisk pace.
wa_dragontail_peak_serpentine_arete.descent_text: From the summit, most parties head down the loose sandy gully shared with the top of Backbone Ridge, boot-ski or downclimb the upper Snow Creek Glacier snowfield where present, then traverse to Aasgard Pass (7,841 ft) and descend its steep, loose talus/scree back to Colchuck Lake. Crampons and an ice axe are important for this descent whenever snow/ice remain on the upper mountain or in Aasgard Pass. Some parties instead reverse via Colchuck Glacier/Col — route-find carefully, as the descent gully is loose and cliffs out if the wrong line is taken.
wa_dragontail_peak_serpentine_arete.name: Serpentine Arête

wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead d
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.descent_text: Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, d
wa_east_twin_needle_south_route.name: South Route

wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges.approach: Start at the Boston Basin trailhead off the Cascade River Road. A steep climbers' trail with several creek crossings (Boston Creek can run high on warm afternoons) climbs to the camps in Boston Basin; overnight stays there need a park backcountry permit. From the upper basin, head north toward Forbidden's South Face and climb the snow slopes and loose gully below and right of it to the East Ridge saddle just northwest of the Solitary Gendarme, about 8,300–8,400 ft. Allow about 4 hours from the trailhead to the saddle, or about 2 hours from the basin camps. Axe and crampons are usually needed for this snow; late in the season they can be left at the saddle.
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges.descent_text: The usual descent is the ascent line reversed. From a horn near the summit, make the first of five single-rope rappels (roughly 400 ft total) down the northeast side to a series of ledges, then follow the ledges east - mostly 3rd class with short 4th-class moves at rib crossings - across roughly five rock ribs before a short gully leads back up to the East Ridge crest near the solitary gendarme. There is no easy way off Forbidden Peak - this line is unprotectable in places and has had a fatality (1975) on the ledge traverse. Cairns (a higher and lower option at most rib crossings) mark the easiest line; recent parties describe the terrain as more straightforward than its reputation suggests when the cairned line is followed carefully, but conditions and route-finding difficulty vary by party experience and weather. From the gendarme, continue down the East Ridge's standard gully system to Boston Basin.
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ledges.name: East Ledges

wa_forbidden_peak_east_ridge.approach: Same trailhead and Boston Basin climbers' trail as the West Ridge (old Diamond Mine roadbed for ~1 mile, then a steep climbers' path with several creek crossings to treeline around 5,300 ft, then talus/heather to the usual high camp at 6,300–6,600 ft, roughly 4–5 miles / 3–4 hours from the car). From camp, rather than crossing toward the south-face couloir, traverse climber's-left/east around the basin and gain the ridges and gullies flanking the glacier on Forbidden's east side (sometimes loosely called the 'Unnamed Glacier'). This leg is notably loose and slower going than the West Ridge approach: expect a few hours of travel over choss-covered slabs, loose rock and seepage, and several small stream crossings, often finishing with a snow gully that wants crampons/microspikes to gain the upper benches below the ridge. Continue up broken rock and snow slopes to the notch that marks the start of the technical East Ridge climbing — roughly 5–6 hours and 5,000+ ft above the trailhead, noticeably longer and more route-finding-intensive than reaching the West Ridge notch.
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: The East Ridge is not reversed as a rappel line in its own right; two descents are used instead. The standard one is the East Ledges, dropping climber's-right/northeast directly off the summit: three rappels trend northeast from the summit area, then a short, exposed grassy traverse east to the next rock rib, followed by two more rappels onto the East Ledges proper, about 5 rappels in all. From there, several hundred metres of loose, sandy and grassy class 3–4 ledges and slabs, marked by intermittent and sometimes doubled cairn lines, lead east above the cliffs over the crevassed Boston Glacier to a gully about 100 ft below the Solitary Gendarme; go up and over the East Ridge through it, then down snow slopes on the south side to the small glacier below Forbidden's south face and the walk back across Boston Basin. The alternative is to reverse along the ridge crest past the gendarmes to the West Ridge notch and descend the West Ridge line: about three rappels on the ridge and about five down the Cat Scratch gullies, roughly eight on a single 60 m rope. It is longer, but it is more travelled and easier to follow, and many parties prefer it to the East Ledges, which are faster but lo
wa_forbidden_peak_east_ridge.name: East Ridge Direct

wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.approach: From Boston Basin Trailhead, hike ~3-4 mi via old mine road then a climbers' path (4 stream crossings) to high camp near 6,400 ft (3-4 hrs). Continue along the moraine and west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col (~7,720 ft) via ~10 ft of 5.7 rock and a Class 3 gully. Rappel into the bergschrund on the far side and climb a short ice wall to gain the Boston Glacier, then traverse west across the Boston Glacier to the base of the Northeast Face below a prominent ice patch.
wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.descent_text: Do not reverse the Northeast Face. Most parties descend by the West Ridge, as below; the East Ledges off the northeast side are the faster but looser, harder-to-follow alternative. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the notch between Forbidden and Torment. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This is a long day; budget extra time given the remote, less-travelled ascent line.
wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.name: Northeast Face

wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face.approach: From Boston Basin Trailhead, hike ~3-4 mi via old mine road then a climbers' path (4 stream crossings) to high camp near 6,400 ft (3-4 hrs), often continuing to a bench at ~7,500 ft beside the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Tower. Ascend the west side of the Quien Sabe Glacier to a notch above Sharkfin Col, rappel onto the Boston Glacier below the bergschrund, traverse the heavily crevassed Boston Glacier, then continue around to the north arm of the Forbidden Glacier. Climb ~900 ft of 30-40+ degree snow/ice to reach the base of the technical rock (5.6 knife-edge ridge leading into the 5.8 crux). Most parties treat this as a 3-day trip.
wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face.descent_text: Do not reverse the Northwest Face; descend by the standard West Ridge. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the West Ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the West Ridge notch. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. From the base, cross back to Boston Basin camp and hike out the climbers' trail. This means NW Face parties do not re-cross the Boston or Forbidden Glaciers or re-climb Sharkfin Col on the way down.
wa_forbidden_peak_northwest_face.name: Northwest Face

wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.approach: From the Boston Basin trailhead off Cascade River Road, follow the unsigned but well-beaten Boston Basin climbers' path. It starts by following the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about 1 mile, then splits off the roadbed to climb steeply and directly through forest. The trail crosses four seasonal creeks/streams (reliable water) as it switchbacks up through increasingly open timber, breaking out above treeline around 5,300 ft. Above treeline it continues into the broad boulder-and-heather Boston Basin cirque, past the usual high-camp sites around 6,300–6,600 ft (roughly 4–5 miles and 3–4 hours from the car, ringed by Sahale, Sharkfin Tower, and Mt. Torment). From camp, make an ascending traverse across talus and the Quien Sabe Glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face; when the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often a faster, drier alternative to crossing snow/ice. Rope up if the glacier is crevassed or snow-covered. Aim for the obvious ~500-ft snow-and-ice couloir splitting the left edge of the south face — the standard gully leading to the West Ridge notch. This couloir steepens to 40–50°+ near its top, typically wants crampons/axe (and sometimes
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: There is no walk-off. Descend the way you came up as far as the notch, then take the rock gullies beside the couloir. From the true summit, downclimb back past the false summit to the crux tower, then work down the ridge crest with exposed 3rd/4th-class downclimbing and about 3 rappels off slung horns and blocks, back to the West Ridge notch. From the notch, downclimb a short section of 3rd-class rock to the first station of the Cat Scratch gullies, the parallel rock chimneys immediately west of the snow couloir. About 5 single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, off fixed anchors on the rib on the down-climber's left, bring you to the snowfield below the south face. Some stations are deliberately short, so do not skip one, and be ready to build an anchor if you cannot find the next. Early season, while the couloir still holds good snow, some parties descend it instead, rappelling the steepest snow to the moat and downclimbing the rest. Watch for the moat again at the bottom. From the base, reverse the glacier-remnant and talus traverse back to Boston Basin camp and out the climbers' trail to the trailhead. The descent is usually slower than the climb: parties report about 1.5 hours bac
wa_forbidden_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.approach: Park at the gravel pull-off (~47.54604, -121.52151, ~1,174 ft). Walk 100-200 yards farther east along the road to the climbers' path leaving on the left at a cairn, then hike about 45 minutes, mostly uphill through forest switchbacks, to the route start near 47.549, -121.5137.
wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.descent_text: Rappel the line. Two 60 m ropes are required — a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for some stations. Reported rappel times run 2.5 to 4 hours. The stations are chained; one station 10 m above the crux anchor lets two 60 m ropes reach the base of the crux pitch in one rappel. Carrying over the top and descending the far side of the mountain has been done but risks an extra night out in brushy, cliffy terrain, and is not recommended. Knot your rope ends: a climber died here on September 7, 2014 after deliberately bypassing a station in fading light, running out of rope, and falling roughly three pitches. Start the rappels with real daylight in hand, and watch for parties still climbing beneath you.
wa_garfield_mountain_infinite_bliss.name: Infinite Bliss

wa_garfield_mountain_leaning_spire_west_.approach: Approach the same as the Main Peak's South Route to 'the Y', then turn up Gully #1 and follow it to the notch below the spire. Midway are 20 ft rock steps, climbable directly or bypassed via loose, brushy scrambling.
wa_garfield_mountain_leaning_spire_west_.descent_text: Descend the line of ascent. A single 70 m rope handles it (60 m would probably work) via five or more rappels off trees and horns, linked by long stretches of downscrambling in the gully. Rappelling off the overhang near the summit into Gully #2 has been done, but getting out to that rappel is described as quite scary and it is not recommended. Below the Y Notch you are back on the Main Peak's South Route descent — a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, then the slab (two double-rope rappels if you rope it) and the dirt gully. Loose rock is the constant theme; the descent is where parties get hurt.
wa_garfield_mountain_leaning_spire_west_.name: Leaning Spire West Route

wa_garfield_mountain_preiss_route.approach: Hike basically straight up, taking a line of least resistance for roughly 1,500 ft while staying left of the lower rocky slabs, with up to 3rd-class scrambling. A 20 ft dirty downclimb leads to the base of the first pitch.
wa_garfield_mountain_preiss_route.descent_text: From the sub-summit, walk down and left through the small gap in the trees onto the gentle northern slope, then go up and over the main West Peak summit and descend the west ridge. Do NOT head straight down the northwest backside slope — the first ascensionist flags this specifically. The alternative, if you have carried two 60 m ropes, is to rappel Infinite Bliss (about 20 rappels off the chain stations); a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for those stations. Either way this is a long descent on brushy, disorienting terrain and should be started with hours of daylight in hand.
wa_garfield_mountain_preiss_route.name: Preiss Route

wa_garfield_mountain_south_route.approach: I-90 Exit 34 near North Bend, then the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56) past the Taylor River bridge junction to a pullout roughly 2.6 miles further on, by a gravel wash. From the car the whole route is only about 1.5 miles horizontally, but 4,400 vertical feet. Start up the dry creek bed and leave it partway up into the woods, following a mix of flagging tape and faint trail up steep pine-needle slopes — 'scrumbling', pulling on whatever vegetation is at hand. About an hour in, at roughly 2,200 ft, you reach the dirt gully. Note that the pine-needle slopes above the slab run about 40 degrees on loose duff; huckleberry stems make good handholds.
wa_garfield_mountain_south_route.descent_text: From the summit scramble down to the top of the easy slab and rig a single-rope rappel to the col at the top of #2 Gully. From there scramble to a bolted rappel station and make the first of about four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes, traversing 100-yard stretches of slab between stations on the east side of the gully; the lower stations are on trees and chockstones with slings dating back to the 1990s. Pack the ropes near the base of the gully and downclimb — this is where the west-side rock is loosest and where a party member was struck by a 500-pound block that cut loose under hand pressure in 2001. Cross back over the Y Notch and the Key Ledge Traverse, make a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, and continue down past the Glade Saddle. Two more double-rope rappels land you at the base of the slab at 2,900 ft; from there it is the wooded ridge, then the dirt gully to the creek at 2,100 ft, then the faint trail and the dry creek bed to the car. Expect to lose the trail in the dark at least once.
wa_garfield_mountain_south_route.name: South Route (Main Peak)

wa_garfield_mountain_southwest_ledges.approach: Leave the climber's path and head into steep forest, continuing upward nearly 1,000 ft through class 4 terrain and thick brush until dropping into a gully on the left; descend several hundred feet to reach the ledge system.
wa_garfield_mountain_southwest_ledges.descent_text: From the summit block reverse the heather benches and downclimb back into the Infinite Bliss line, then rappel the entire route — roughly 20 double-rope rappels off the chain stations with two 60 m ropes, interspersed with downclimbing. A 70 m or 80 m single rope is NOT long enough for the Infinite Bliss stations. Watch for parties climbing below you; the whole descent runs down a gully-slab that funnels anything you dislodge straight onto them. Budget 3-4 hours minimum for the rappels and start them with enough daylight left — a 2014 fatality on this rappel line happened when a climber skipped a station in fading light and rappelled off unknotted rope ends.
wa_garfield_mountain_southwest_ledges.name: Southwest Ledges

wa_gilbert_peak_meade_glacier.approach: Drive to the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead (Trail #1120, elev. ~4,044 ft): from Naches, WA take US-12 W about 22 miles, turn onto Forest Road 1200 (Tieton Reservoir Road) for 4.5 miles, then onto Forest Road 1000 (South Fork Tieton Road) for 12.6 miles to the trailhead at road's end (last ~7 miles gravel, generally in good condition). Hike Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows (crossing Conrad Creek) into the Goat Rocks Wilderness, continuing to the Surprise Lake loop. Take the loop's right fork to the trail's high point, then leave the trail and climb west into a basin; pass between a pair of big mounds and descend briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.
wa_gilbert_peak_meade_glacier.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb the short, loose scramble to the small saddle and follow the goat and boot path on the southwest side back to the ridge. Descend the Meade Glacier snowfields past the rock band that splits the upper and lower glacier; glissading is common in early and mid season when the snow is consolidated (self-arrest gear required). Recross the basin to the trail's high point, then follow the Surprise Lake loop and Trail #1120 back through Conrad Meadows to the trailhead.
wa_gilbert_peak_meade_glacier.name: Meade Glacier

wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.approach: Drive to the Berry Patch or Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (Chambers Lake area) off Forest Road 21/2150 on the west side of the Goat Rocks: turn east onto FR 21, continue about 13 miles, turn at the Snowgrass Trail/Chambers Lake sign onto FR 2150, then follow signs to the Snowgrass Flat Trailhead (elev. ~4,650 ft). Hike Trail #96 (Snowgrass) roughly 4 miles and ~2,000 ft of gain along Goat Creek toward Snowgrass Flats, a large subalpine meadow that is closed to camping (use the established sites below it); from there reach the PCT (via Trail #96 or the cutoff Trail #97) and follow it southbound about 2 miles to Cispus Basin, which has an established camp in the trees just above the PCT's Cispus River crossing. Climb to the saddle at the basin's northeast end, then scramble east across the Goat Ledges/Goat Ribs traverse toward Gilbert Peak (often combined with Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak in one traverse day).
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.descent_text: Downclimb the Class 2-3 summit section back through the notch behind the black prow, then carefully retrace the white aggregate band across the Goat Ribs/Goat Ledges at the same ~7,500 ft traverse elevation used on ascent to minimize rockfall exposure to teammates below. From the saddle, descend into Cispus Basin, follow the PCT back to Trail #96 (or the cutoff Trail #97), and descend Trail #96 to the trailhead.
wa_gilbert_peak_west_route.name: West Route

wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (2,050 ft, off FR 49/Sloan Creek Road), hike ~9 mi to White Pass on the PCT. Continue east on the Foam Creek Trail ~2 mi, cross a ridge saddle near 6,600 ft, then traverse the White Chuck Glacier basin trending NE to Glacier Gap (~7,300 ft), the standard high camp where the Suiattle and White Chuck glaciers meet. Summit day is roughly 7 mi round trip with about 3,450 ft of gain, some of it height lost and regained along the way: climb gentle snow above camp, follow a climber's track on volcanic scree onto the Gerdine and Cool glaciers, end-run a crevasse or two, then rejoin the climber's trail for the final steep pitch to the summit.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.descent_text: No rappelling; reverse the ascent line on foot. From the summit, descend the ridge to the 9,600 ft col, then down the Cool Glacier to the 9,100 ft col. On the traverse back beneath Disappointment Peak, keep lower and farther from the face than on the way in to cut the time spent under its rockfall. Crevasses on the Cool Glacier open wider as summer goes on and snow bridges weaken, so stay roped and probe suspect bridges. From Glacier Gap, return across the White Chuck basin to White Pass and out the North Fork Sauk River Trail.
wa_glacier_peak_cool_glacier_gerdine.name: Disappointment Peak Cleaver (Gerdine Ridge / Cool Glacier)

wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.approach: Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via the White Chuck River, no longer usable since a 2003 flood destroyed the trail and road: the old line followed the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing (water) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT on Glacier Ridge about 0.7 miles beyond the creek, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. (2) Via North Fork Sauk Trailhead: North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass (~9 miles, ~5,900 ft), then a long traverse north on/near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area — a 20-mile-plus approach day used by some parties. From high camp, the route proper begins by traversing the upper southwest slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to an 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers. Ascend the Kennedy Glacier — a 'crumbling mess' of loose moraine and boulders low down — to an 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.descent_text: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — once on the ridge there is no turning back — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT, then south on the PCT to White Pass and down the North Fork Sauk Trail to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: there is a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock
wa_glacier_peak_frostbite_ridge.name: Frostbite Ridge

wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.approach: Standard historical approach: from the White Chuck River Trailhead (FS-23, closed to vehicles at milepost 3.7 after flood damage; check status), follow trail #643 about 4 miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the PCT; turn left (north) and follow the PCT about 2 miles to the Glacier Creek crossing and campsites (pack-in time 4-5 hours). An alternate approach via the North Fork Sauk Trail and PCT over Red Pass to Glacier Creek is also used and is the open option while FS-23 stays closed.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.descent_text: Besides reversing the ascent line, the standard alternate descent goes via Frostbite Ridge: traverse past the distinctive 'Rabbit Ears' rock formation, then descend the (separate) Vista Glacier back down to the lower Kennedy Glacier and Kennedy Ridge camp, watching for opened crevasses and softening snow bridges throughout.
wa_glacier_peak_kennedy_glacier.name: Kennedy Glacier

wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.approach: From the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (off Sloan Creek Road, FR 49), follow North Fork Sauk Trail #649 up the valley through old-growth forest, past the Red Creek bridge to Mackinaw Shelter, then up a long series of switchbacks to meet the Pacific Crest Trail at about 5,950 ft, roughly 8-9 miles from the car. White Pass and its camp are a short way south along the PCT; this route does not go there. Turn north on the PCT and cross Red Pass (about 6,500 ft) a mile or two on, then descend into the upper White Chuck valley and follow the PCT down it for roughly 7-9 miles, past the old White Chuck River Trail junction (~3,850 ft), to a forested campsite near 4,100 ft beside Sitkum Creek. There, leave the maintained trail on the unsigned, unmaintained climbers' path (closer to a rough angler's path than a real trail), which goes straight up the forested ridge south of Sitkum Creek to Boulder Basin (5,500-6,000 ft), where the trees break and the standard high camp sits on heather and rock benches with running water nearby. From camp, ascend snowfields southeast onto the toe of the Sitkum Glacier. The old approach up the White Chuck River Trail past Kennedy Hot Springs to the same PCT j
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT at Sitkum Creek, then walk the PCT back up the White Chuck valley and over Red Pass to the North Fork Sauk Trail and the trailhead.
wa_glacier_peak_sitkum_glacier.name: Sitkum Glacier

wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.approach: From the Goat Mountain Trailhead (day-use parking just off FS-32/Hannegan Pass Rd, ~2.1-2.3 mi up from the Glacier Public Service Center), follow Goat Mountain Trail #673. It's a well-built but relentlessly steep trail that gains the ridge via dozens of switchbacks, crossing a small cascading creek/waterfall repeatedly in the first mile through old-growth fir and hemlock (look for ~100-year-old fire-scarred cedar snags). Around 1 mi (~3,200 ft) the grade eases and the trail traverses onto a narrow side-hill ridge. At roughly 2 mi the trail crosses into Mount Baker Wilderness; just past the boundary sign an unsigned spur ('Old Goat Trail') splits east toward an old lookout site - stay on the main tread. Big views of Baker, Shuksan, and Sefrit open through meadows by 2.7 mi, and the maintained trail tops out on the ridge crest at a 5,200-ft viewpoint knob around mile 4, with the official terminus near 5,600 ft (~4.1 mi, ~3,100 ft gain). Beyond this point the route leaves maintained tread and becomes an open ridge boot path: continue about 0.8 mi and 1,000 ft more to the ~6,600-ft West Peak false summit. Snow lingers here well into summer (reports note solid snow from ~4,300-4,500 ft)
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling anywhere on the route - reverse the ascent line exactly. Downclimb the mixed snow/rock crux back to the col, climb back over (or bypass around, staying off the cornices) the West Peak false summit, and regain the boot path down to the official trail terminus near 5,600 ft. From there, follow Goat Mountain Trail #673's switchbacks back down through the meadows, past the wilderness-boundary/Old Goat Trail junction, and through the old-growth section to the trailhead. Carry an ice axe and know self-arrest for both directions of travel on the snow sections: afternoon sun can soften the snowfields significantly (increasing slip and post-holing risk on the way down), while morning refreeze can leave the same slopes firm enough to want careful cramponing. Give cornices along the ridge crest a wide margin on the way down as well - they are easy to underestimate from above and have caused parties to detour off-route.
wa_goat_mountain_south_ridge.name: South Ridge / Standard Scramble

wa_this_my_friend.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction with Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A at 2.6 miles, then continue to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3-4.4 miles and about 2,200 ft of gain. From the lake's south side, pick up the Aasgard Pass climbers' trail and ascend roughly 85% of the pass's height to about 7,250 ft (roughly 1,700 ft above the lake, most of the way up the pass's total ~2,200 ft), where the main trail crosses a large braided creek - the pass's primary water source, though it can thin out by late summer. Continue 5-10 minutes past this crossing, then leave the established trail between 7,300-7,400 ft and pick a rising traverse rightward across loose, unstable scree to the base of the route, about 300 ft below where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail. This off-trail scree section is the crux hazard of the approach - loose, exposed underfoot, and consequential given the terrain below.
wa_this_my_friend.descent_text: From the top, traverse south and west across broken 3rd/4th class terrain, losing elevation gradually until reaching a clean gully roughly 500 ft below the final belay. Descend the gully to a large ledge, then scramble southwest to walkable ground where you intersect the standard summit descent trail down to Aasgard Pass; follow the cairned, braided climbers' trail down the pass's steep talus/snow (~2,200 ft in under a mile) back to Colchuck Lake, favoring climbers' left near the granite walls and watching for the common error of drifting climbers' right into cliffed terrain near Colchuck Peak. Crampons/axe are worth carrying into mid-summer for the Aasgard Pass snow. This is a walk-off descent - the route is not set up for rappel.
wa_this_my_friend.name: This, My Friend
